claims.text: Controlled co-alloying with Al, Cr, and Si improves the high-temperature oxidation resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Al, Cr, and Si additions promote formation of a continuous protective oxide scale on refractory high-entropy alloys.
The protective oxide scale produced by these additions is adherent.
The protective scale retards oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
An untreated W-based or Nb-based refractory high-entropy alloy exhibits significant oxide-scale spallation and mass gain during high-temperature exposure.
The intervention is expected to work in air at 1000–1100 °C for exposures of 50–200 hours.
The resulting scale is composed primarily of Al2O3 and Cr2O3, with possible contributions from silicon-derived oxides.
The oxide scale enhances scale adhesion and limits oxygen ingress.
During high-temperature exposure, the added Al, Cr, and Si preferentially oxidize.
Preferential oxidation of Al, Cr, and Si produces stable, slow-growing protective oxide layers.
The protective layers decrease the oxidation rate relative to the untreated alloy.
The modified alloy will have lower mass gain than the untreated alloy under identical exposure conditions.
The modified alloy will show improved scale adhesion and reduced spallation relative to the untreated alloy.
The untreated alloy develops a less continuous and more spall-prone oxide layer, leading to higher mass gain and degradation.
The oxidation benefit depends on using optimized or proper amounts of Al, Cr, and Si.
Excessive Al, Cr, and Si additions may form brittle intermetallic compounds and impair mechanical integrity.
The exact quantitative oxidation improvement and optimal Al, Cr, and Si concentrations in refractory high-entropy alloys remain undetermined.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant mass-gain reduction, exemplified as greater than 20%, together with improved scale continuity and adhesion after 200 hours at 1100 °C in air would falsify the hypothesis.
